title: On the phone
job: Calls and messages — openings, closings, taking a message
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: estar plus -ando or -iendo says something is happening right now: estoy comiendo. Spanish keeps it for the actual moment — for tomorrow it uses the plain present, which is M6's rule.
Me llamo is "my name is" and te llamo is "I'll call you". Same verb, and the little pronoun in front decides which. A learner who has said me llamo for two levels will read te llamo as "I name you".
le names the person something is done TO or FOR — le dejo un mensaje. It is the same le that made le gusta read the way it does.
Identifying yourself on the phone is Soy + your name, exactly as English says "it's me". No extra word is needed.
está does a third job here: ¿Está tu hermana? asks whether she is THERE, not how she is. The verb has not changed; the situation supplies the meaning.

words.note: The polite imperative of decir, built from digo exactly as siga is from sigo. It is how Spain answers a phone; dígame is the longer, slightly warmer version.
Carries an accent because it asks, like qué and dónde. Its unaccented twin quien joins clauses and is not taught here.

sentences.trap: Diga is not "say it". On a phone it is simply hello, and translating it word for word makes it sound like an order.
sentences.sound: DI-ga with a hard g. DEE-ga-me for the longer form, stressed on the first syllable and written with an accent.

variations.changed: the longer opener, which is commoner in Spain
the question and its answer together
the caller checking they have the right number

mistake.why: dice is "he says". The phone answer is the imperative: Diga.

sentences.usage: Spain. Much of Latin America says ¿Aló? or ¿Bueno? instead, and both are understood.
sentences.mnemonic: Spain picks up the phone by inviting you to speak.

sentences.cue: It's Rohan, is your sister there?

words.note: No accent: tu hermana is "your sister". The accented tú is the pronoun, and the two are different words on the page and identical in the ear.

sentences.trap: está here asks whether she is present, not how she is. Same verb, different question, and only the situation tells them apart.
sentences.sound: TU, one syllable, and the accent on the pronoun changes nothing you can hear.

variations.cue: It's Ana, is your brother there?
variations.changed: another caller and another sibling
por favor, which softens a call to a house
the other job of estar, in the next breath

mistake.why: es would be asking whether she IS your sister. Being present is estar: ¿está tu hermana?

sentences.usage: Calling a house. Naming yourself first is expected, and skipping it reads as abrupt.
sentences.mnemonic: está asks if they are there; es asks who they are.

sentences.cue: One moment, she's coming to the phone.

words.note: Right now, or in a moment — Spanish uses it for both, and ahora mismo is the emphatic one.

sentences.trap: se pone is not M5's ¿me pone…? The little se turns "put" into "put oneself", which on a phone means come to it.
sentences.sound: a-O-ra, three syllables with the h silent, and one tapped r.

variations.cue: One moment, I'll call her now.
variations.changed: a different way of handling the call

variations.cue: She can't right now, I'm sorry.
variations.changed: the refusal, with M1's apology
S05's -iendo form, giving the reason

mistake.why: Without se the sentence says she is putting something. se pone is coming to the phone.

sentences.usage: What the person who answered says as they go to fetch someone.
sentences.mnemonic: se turns putting into putting yourself.

words.note: hablar with -ando on the end. Every -ar verb makes this shape the same way, and estar in front of it says the action is happening now.

sentences.trap: hablar con, not hablar a. You talk WITH someone in Spanish, even when English says "to".
sentences.sound: a-BLAN-do, with the h silent and the b soft between vowels.

variations.changed: the I-form of estar in front
someone else on the other end
two -ndo forms set against each other

mistake.why: hablar takes con for the person you talk to: hablando con mi madre.

sentences.usage: The reason someone cannot come to the phone. It is happening at this instant, which is what the form is for.
sentences.mnemonic: -ar verbs take -ando, and estar puts them in this moment.

sentences.cue: I'm eating, I'll call you later.

words.note: An -er or -ir verb takes -iendo where an -ar verb takes -ando: comiendo, bebiendo, escribiendo.
llamar, to call. Me llamo is "my name is" and te llamo is "I'll call you" — the same verb, and the little word in front decides.
The bare word inside M10's hasta luego, doing its own job at last.

sentences.trap: te llamo is a promise about the future said in the present, exactly as M6 taught. And it is not "I name you".
sentences.sound: ko-MYEN-do. YA-mo for llamo, because ll is a y almost everywhere.

variations.cue: I'm eating, I'll call you tomorrow.
variations.changed: a named time instead of luego
ahora making the moment explicit

variations.cue: I'll call you on Friday, OK?
variations.changed: M6's vale closing the arrangement

mistake.why: me llamo says your name. To promise a call it is te llamo.

sentences.usage: The commonest way any Spanish phone call ends early.
sentences.mnemonic: me names you, te calls you.

sentences.cue: Shall I leave her a message?

words.note: Names the person something is done TO or FOR, and it does not say which gender. It is the same le that sits inside le gusta.
dejar, to leave something behind. Not the same as leaving a place, which is a different verb.
Masculine despite the -e: un mensaje. The j is the same breathy h as in lejos.

sentences.trap: le covers him and her alike. Spanish marks the role and not the gender here, which is the opposite of what English does.
sentences.sound: men-SA-he, with the j said as a breathy h and the final e always sounded.

variations.display: ¿Le dejo un mensaje a tu hermana?

said flat, it becomes what you are going to do

variations.cue: Could you leave me a message?
variations.changed: me instead of le, and the usted form of the verb

mistake.why: le goes in front of the conjugated verb, like every pronoun in this course: ¿Le dejo…?

sentences.usage: Offered by whoever answered. The caller says sí, por favor and then dictates it.
sentences.mnemonic: le is a role, not a gender.

sentences.cue: Can you give me your number?

words.note: Masculine: el número. The accent is on the first syllable and is written because that is unusual for a word ending in a vowel.

sentences.trap: The accent on número is not optional. Without it the word would be stressed on the middle syllable and would be a verb.
sentences.sound: NU-me-ro — three syllables, stressed on the first, which is what the accent marks.

variations.cue: Could you give me your number, please?
variations.changed: the usted verb, with por favor softening it

variations.cue: Can you give me your home number?
variations.changed: de naming which number
tu in front of a different sentence

mistake.why: The accent is part of the spelling: número. Dropping it moves the stress and the word.

sentences.usage: Ending a first conversation. Spanish asks directly and it is not forward.
sentences.mnemonic: The accent holds the stress at the front.

sentences.display: No está, llama luego, por favor.
sentences.cue: She isn't in, call later, please.

words.note: The tú imperative of llamar, and it is spelled exactly like the he-she form. For most verbs the friendly command IS the third-person present. The row for llamar is S05's.

sentences.trap: llama is both "he calls" and "call!". Only the sentence tells them apart, and Spanish is comfortable with that.
sentences.sound: YA-ma. The double l is one sound, never two.

variations.cue: She isn't in, call on Friday.

the place named

mistake.why: llamas is a statement — "you call". The command drops the -s: llama.

sentences.usage: Said by whoever answered, and it is not rude. Spanish gives instructions more directly than English does.
sentences.mnemonic: The friendly command is the he-form.

words.note: Describes something that has been got wrong, so it agrees with what it describes: número equivocado, casa equivocada.

sentences.usage: Said and heard in a second, and then the call ends. Perdone is what keeps it civil.
sentences.mnemonic: The number is wrong, so the adjective follows the number.

words.note: The partner of M1's me, and on this verb it is what separates a promise from a name: te llamo is "I'll call you", me llamo is "my name is".

sentences.trap: Everything here is recombination: M6's vale, M6's arrangement present, and this module's te llamo. No new word, and that is the point of the last sentence.

variations.cue: I'll call you on Friday, OK?

mistake.why: The present carries a settled plan: te llamo mañana. A future tense here sounds like a forecast.

sentences.usage: How half of all Spanish calls end. ¿vale? asks for agreement without asking a question.
sentences.mnemonic: Promise it in the present and seal it with vale.
